conclusions.basis: DESE’s Chapter 70 key factors workbook, FY2007 to FY2026: the municipal contribution sheet for Lunenburg minus the district aid sheet for Lunenburg Public Schools, year by year. Checked against DESE’s own apportionment sheet as Monty Tech reprinted it in its FY2027 budget presentation, and against three figures the district’s business director gave the Finance Committee in three different years.
conclusions.claim: The single amount the state requires Lunenburg to pay for schools, split between two districts
conclusions.detail: A Lunenburg child enrolling at Monty Tech does not add to what the town has to raise for schools. It moves part of it: the state sets ONE required contribution for the whole town and splits it between the town’s two districts. In FY2026 that single town-wide requirement was $14,605,342, of which Monty Tech’s share was $1,270,711 and Lunenburg Public Schools’ $13,334,631. The town-wide total is the lesser of what the state calculates from Lunenburg’s property values and resident income and a cap on the local share of its foundation budget — and the wealth figure is the binding one in all 20 years DESE publishes, so enrollment never enters it. The split is each district’s share of the town’s foundation budget, and that identity holds to a tenth of a basis point in 19 of those years.
conclusions.not_shown: That the town is therefore indifferent to where a child enrolls. The state sets a larger foundation budget for a vocational pupil than for one in the town’s own schools, so a move shifts more than a proportionate slice of the bill; the assessment also carries transportation and capital above the state minimum, which the district apportions by enrollment and not by foundation budget; and nothing here says what Lunenburg’s own schools stop spending when a child leaves.

conclusions.so_what: A child moving to Monty Tech does not add to the town’s bill. It moves part of it.

conclusions.basis: the district’s own FY2027 budget presentation — its “FY 2027 Budget Summary” page for the budget, the Chapter 70 estimate and the total assessed on all eighteen towns, and its member-town apportionment sheet for Lunenburg’s own line. The town’s side is its MUNIS year-to-date budget report, general fund, which carries the same total to the cent.
conclusions.claim: Billed to Lunenburg for Monty Tech, which is not what a place there costs
conclusions.detail: What Lunenburg is billed for Monty Tech is not what a Monty Tech place costs. The town’s $1,334,521 is 3.9% of the district’s budget while Lunenburg’s children are 6.8% of its foundation enrollment. Monty Tech’s FY2026 budget is $34,641,344. Chapter 70 aid paid straight to the district covers 54.2% of it, and assessments on all eighteen member towns together cover 38.0%; the rest is the district’s own receipts, and none of that appears in Lunenburg’s bill. So this line measures what the town raises, and it can move in a year when nothing at the school costs any more or any less.
conclusions.not_shown: What a Lunenburg place at Monty Tech costs. This archive holds two of the district’s budget books and no series, no all-funds report after a year closed, and nothing that attributes any of the district’s spending to one member town’s children. The bill can be tracked; the cost cannot.
conclusions.so_what: State aid paid straight to the school covers most of its budget, and none of that is in this bill.

conclusions.basis: the five-year forecast of this line printed in a Select Board packet in January 2021, read as a series out of the minutes, against the town’s MUNIS ledger for the last year of it and against the DESE-derived required-contribution series for the same span.
conclusions.claim: The actual Monty Tech bill, against a forecast that carried it forward at an inflation rate
conclusions.detail: This line cannot be planned as an ordinary cost escalator. Carried forward at 2.5% a year it reached $1,005,464 for FY2026, and the assessment came in at $1,334,521. Over the same span the state-required minimum inside the assessment compounded at 9.3% a year, and Monty Tech’s share of the town’s foundation budget — the fraction that decides how much of one town-wide requirement lands here — went from 7.2% to 8.7%. Neither of those is a price, and neither is inside an inflation assumption. A town that wants this line forecast has to forecast the Chapter 70 formula and the split, which is a different exercise and a harder one.
conclusions.not_shown: Why the projection was built that way, or that any other rate would have been better. It is one packet, it states a series and no method, and nothing here establishes what was assumed. What is established is that the quantity being projected is set by a state formula rather than by a price.

gaps.closes: Monty Tech’s annual budget book for each year, presented to its own School Committee and to the Lunenburg Finance Committee every March, and DESE’s End of Year Financial Report for LEA 08320000, which gives all-funds spending by function in dollars after the year closes.
gaps.what: What Monty Tech spends, and on what
gaps.why: Lunenburg is assessed $1,334,521 for Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical in FY2026 and that figure is what the town is BILLED, not what educating 101 foundation pupils costs. PART OF THIS ROW HAS CLOSED. DESE’s RADAR district comparison publishes an all-funds per-pupil total for LEA 08320000 for FY2009 to FY2025 — seventeen consecutive years, every one of them summing to the workbook’s own printed in-district total — so the district’s per-pupil spending CAN now be tracked over time and set beside Lunenburg Public Schools’ own, measured the same way, which is what /what-other-districts-spend does. WHAT REMAINS OPEN is the composition and the attribution. RADAR gives ten per-pupil function columns and no dollars, no fund split and nothing specific to Lunenburg’s children; the archive holds two of the district’s own budget books — the FY2024 hearing book and the FY2027 presentation — so a FY24-to-FY27 view by DESE function code exists in dollars, with no year before FY2024 and nothing for the years between the two books. So what the district spends on a Lunenburg child, as against on any child, is still not established.

gaps.closes: the district’s annual assessment certification to each member town, which states the four components separately; the Town Accountant receives one every year and the district retains all of them.
gaps.what: How the Monty Tech assessment splits between operating, transportation and capital
gaps.why: A regional assessment is four parts, and the district names them: required minimum contribution set by the state, transportation and other operating above minimum net school spending, capital outlay, and bonds. The split is published for FY2024, FY2026 and FY2027 in the district’s own budget books, and for FY2023 it was itemised in prose at a Finance Committee meeting. Every other year holds only the total. That includes FY2025, and it includes all eleven annual-report years FY2011 to FY2022 — so for the whole of the series this project charts, the roughly 4-10% of the assessment sitting above the state minimum cannot be attributed to transportation, to capital or to debt. It matters because those three behave nothing alike: one tracks a busing contract, one is voted year by year, and one is fixed until it ends.

gaps.closes: the district’s FY2027 assessment certification to the Town of Lunenburg, and the Monty Tech line as finally voted at Annual Town Meeting.
gaps.what: Why the district and the town state different FY2027 Monty Tech assessments
gaps.why: Monty Tech’s FY2027 budget presentation puts Lunenburg’s total assessment at $1,452,379, built from a required minimum contribution of $1,378,183 and a transportation and operating assessment of $74,196 with no capital and no bonds. The Town’s own FY2027 operating budget book carries the same line at $1,452,426, in all three of its scenarios. The difference is $47 and neither document acknowledges the other. It is small enough to be a rounding or a late revision and it is not nothing: the two figures are the district’s bill and the town’s appropriation for the same year, and every other year in this archive where both exist ties to the dollar or to eighteen cents.

gaps.closes: the Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School District regional agreement and its amendments, filed with the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education and held by the district and by each member town’s clerk.
gaps.what: How the Montachusett regional agreement apportions costs among its member towns
gaps.why: The apportionment method is now on the record twice: the district printed it in Lunenburg’s FY2017 annual town report — four parts, with transportation and other operating divided by each town’s 1 October enrollment share and capital divided by each town’s school-attending children in grades 1 to 12 — and DESE’s own apportionment sheet, reprinted in the FY2027 budget presentation, shows the required-contribution part split between a town’s two districts by foundation-budget share. WHAT IS STILL MISSING IS THE INSTRUMENT. A budget book states current practice; the regional agreement is what binds it, and it is the document that would say whether the ratios can be changed, how bonds are apportioned and over what term, what a member town’s withdrawal would require, and what amendments have been made. Asked at the Finance Committee on 5 February 2026 whether the agreement was indefinite or could be renegotiated, the Superintendent-Director said he believed it was ongoing and that amendments were very rare. A recollection at a meeting is not the instrument.

gaps.closes: Monty Tech’s admissions summary by sending town and year — applications received, offers made, waitlisted — which the district produces for its own School Committee.
gaps.what: How many Lunenburg applicants Monty Tech turns away
gaps.why: Lunenburg’s count at Monty Tech has risen in nine of the last twelve years, and a count is the outcome of two things at once: families applying, and Monty Tech admitting. The lottery exists precisely because more apply than there are places. Asked at the Finance Committee on 5 February 2026 how many Lunenburg students were turned away, the district’s business manager said she was unsure of the exact number. The Class of 2030 lottery result in this archive gives one cohort’s admissions — 24 Lunenburg students of 365 places — and its per-applicant pages are OCR of an image PDF and cannot be counted from. So a rising count cannot be read as rising demand, and the two have opposite implications for what the town should expect next.

gaps.closes: DESE’s foundation enrollment detail for the Chapter 70 calculation, which states the collection date and the categories included, published beside the key factors workbook this project already holds.
gaps.what: Why DESE’s foundation enrollment for Lunenburg at Monty Tech differs from its own October headcount
gaps.why: Two DESE counts of the same thing disagree in every year. The Chapter 70 foundation enrollment used to compute the assessment — derived on /monty-tech by subtracting the Lunenburg district’s from the town’s — runs between eight below and fifteen above the October headcount of Lunenburg residents attending Montachusett Regional in DESE’s own residents-by-district file, and the gap has no consistent sign or size. One documented mechanism puts children into the assessment who are not at Monty Tech: the district’s business director told the Finance Committee in March 2022 that four Lunenburg students attending trade programmes at Leominster and Nashoba “become part of the Monty Tech assessment”. That accounts for a difference in one direction and not for the years running the other way. Until it is reconciled, no per-student figure on this page can be quoted without saying which count is the denominator.

not_established: What Monty Tech spends over time, or what a Lunenburg place there costs. The assessment is what the town is BILLED. The archive holds two of the district’s own budget books — FY2024 and FY2027 — and no series, no year before FY2024, and no all-funds figure reported after a year closed. So the bill can be tracked and the cost cannot.

How the assessment divides between operating, transportation and capital in FY2025, or in any of the eleven annual-report years. The four-part split is published for FY2024, FY2026 and FY2027 and stated in prose at a meeting for FY2023. Everywhere else only the total exists.

That the eleven annual-report figures are right. Every one of them fails the extractor’s own reconciliation, so they are drawn as candidates. What can be said is that each sits above the independently derived state minimum by a margin consistent with transportation and capital — which is a check on their shape, not a check on their values.

Why the district’s FY2027 assessment and the Town’s FY2027 budget line differ by $47. Both are in the archive, neither mentions the other, and every other year where two figures exist ties to the dollar or to eighteen cents.

Why the number of Lunenburg children at Monty Tech has risen. A count is the outcome of families applying and of Monty Tech admitting, and the lottery exists precisely because more apply than can be admitted. Nothing here separates demand from capacity, and the district told the Finance Committee in February 2026 that it did not know how many Lunenburg students had been turned away.

Why DESE’s foundation enrollment and DESE’s own October headcount of Lunenburg residents at Monty Tech disagree in every year, by between eight below and fifteen above. Both are published; nothing reconciles them, so every per-student figure on this page names its denominator.

That the town could reduce the assessment by deciding to. Roughly 95% of it is the Chapter 70 minimum required local contribution, computed by the state from Lunenburg’s property value and resident income and apportioned by foundation budget. No Lunenburg vote sets it, and no Lunenburg vote admits or refuses a child to the school.

What the regional agreement says. The apportionment METHOD is on the record — the district printed it in the FY2017 annual town report — but the instrument that binds it is not in this archive, so nothing here can say whether the ratios can be changed, how bonds would be apportioned, or what withdrawing from the district would involve.

said.quote: 96 percent of the Monty Tech assessment is governed by the state, which determines contribution by average income and property values in town
said.why: The mechanism, said out loud to the Finance Committee in 2022. The DESE workbook agrees with the shape of it: in FY2023 the state-required minimum was 96.0% of what the town appropriated, and the remaining 4.0% was itemised in the same presentation as transportation and capital.

said.quote: foundation enrollment has increased from 83 to 94, which increases the town’s required minimum contribution to $1,012,282 (a $140,597 increase) for Monty Tech, which is 8.2 percent of all L
said.why: Two of the four figures this page checks its own derivation against. Subtracting the school district’s required local contribution from the town’s, in DESE’s workbook, gives 83 and 94 foundation pupils and $1,012,282 — independently, from a document neither party wrote.

said.quote: DESE determines how much local communities contribute using their calculations and formula. The calculation includes half the income for town residents and half of the value of the property value in the town
said.why: Said four years later, about the same formula. It is why the town’s total obligation does not move when a child changes school: the inputs are property value and resident income.

said.quote: what if anything can be done to reduce the contribution that Lunenburg needs to pay. Tom Brown states there is potential to change but that requires a change to the formula
said.who: a Finance Committee member and the Superintendent-Director
said.why: The question this page exists to answer, asked at a public meeting, and answered the same way the arithmetic answers it.

said.quote: Chris Menard inquires about the district agreement whether it’s indeﬁnite or if it can be renegotiated. Tom Brown believes the agreement is ongoing. He is also aware of some amendments, but they are very rare.
said.who: a Finance Committee member and the Superintendent-Director
said.why: The nearest thing in the record to the regional agreement itself, which this archive does not hold. It is a recollection given at a meeting, not the document, and it is printed here as that.

said.quote: The total contribution needed from Lunenburg is $1,270,711.
said.why: The third check on the derivation, for FY2026, to the dollar. It is also the figure a reader is most likely to mistake for the assessment: the town appropriated more than this, and the difference is transportation and capital.

said.quote: totaling $1,127,113 going to Monty Tech, which amounts to 6.62 percent of Monty Tech’s operating budget
said.why: The fourth check, for FY2024 — and rule 11 in one line from the other direction: what Lunenburg is billed is a small share of what the district spends, because Chapter 70 and everything else on its revenue side pay the rest.

said.quote: a reduction in the Monty Tech Assessment will cover that cost
said.why: The one year in twelve where the appropriation candidate does NOT sit comfortably above the state-required minimum. An assessment certified downward mid-year is a thing that happens to this line, and it is a reason to read a single year of it carefully.

said.quote: The Monty Tech Assessment stands at $117,858.00, leaving $1,256,405.89 to be allocated between the School and Town budgets
said.why: Two quantities are called “the Monty Tech Assessment” in the town’s own record and they differ by a factor of eleven. This one is the INCREASE taken off new revenue before the rest is split — the arithmetic in the sentence proves it — and the assessment itself is the larger figure this page charts.

said.quote: we'd have to disentangle ourselves from Monty Tech
said.why: Said at a School Committee meeting in March 2026, about bringing vocational programmes back into Lunenburg’s own schools. It is the only place in the searched record where leaving the district is raised, and it is printed because the page owes a reader who is thinking about it the arithmetic rather than a verdict.

said.quote: The Committee agrees that Monty Techs assessment should be aligned with the Lunenberg Public Schools
said.why: What the Finance Committee wants the line to do. Whether it can be made to do that is the subject of this page: the state-required part is 95% of it and is set by a formula the town is not a party to.
